500+ employees!
But here’s the thing about this CEO.  It wasn’t easy for them to get there. They’re not a unicorn founder, or an ex-VP of Sales or something like that. They did it themselves.
And they came from nowhere.
I know many folks might look at their journey and say “wow”. But I also can see the struggles in those 8 years of bootstrapping and so much more.  Because they are real — even if you don’t see them on social media.
How do CEOs like this get to $100m+ ARR?  How does someone that has never sold a single deal at all … go from nothing to closing multi-million dollar deals with the CIO of a Fortune 500 company?

And then a second one.
And then a third.
And each of these deals helped HubSpot learn more about what the enterprise needed in terms of software, and how to build it — all while still just 40 employees!
But here’s where things get tricky.  If you are growing too fast … if you don’t understand what the Social Contract is with an Enterprise buyer …. then you can blow up a deal.
For example, if your sales team has no way to manage an enterprise contract once it closes — that contract blows up and never gets paid.

So what’s the social contract?  It means you have to be honest about how many people are on your team.

So just this week we had the most recent IPO — of Monday.com.  A big one!  At least for those that follow SaaS.
Monday is a great company, and now it’s public:
It has over 300 employees
That do not make any money at all (i.e., in R&D)
And just recently crossed $500m+ ARR with almost zero churn!
So what can we learn from Monday?  A lot.  Let me try to distill some of the key takeaways:
1. Yes, going multi-product is still possible
If you’ve seen a lot of great SaaS companies go vertical and stay that way over time — they’re not wrong here.  But there’s also no reason for many of us in SaaS to only do one thing.

Monday.com has had its fair share of issues here — and they’ve been very transparent about them with their public investors.  They just announced the first ever CCO!
4. Monday.com still doesn’t really make any money from R&D, or even Sales & Marketing
A lot of us in SaaS have gotten so used to having our expenses covered by our sales team that we forget this is actually a pretty unusual model.
Monday.com does not yet cover its R&D costs with revenue — and it hasn’t for years.  It doesn’t make any money from marketing either, at least as far as I can tell.

Monday has been on an epic journey. From its first customers in Israel to being one of the leading enterprise SaaS companies today. And it’s only gotten more powerful and easier for users.
#1.  More Power Users = Less Revenue Per User
This is a reminder how Monday.com has evolved over time:
In the early days, it was $30-40 per user per month. But in those days, there were often only one or two power users at an SMB. Fast forward to today and you’ll see that SMBs are using more features … but they’re also just paying a fraction of what they used to.
#2.  You Need to Make it Easy for Power Users
Monday’s core customers have gone from 1-20 to 1000+ users, often in an organization, all on Monday.com today. This is a reminder how important ease-of-use and workflows are. Your power-users will become your evangelists.
#3.  Almost Half of Their $550m ARR Is Outside North America
Monday has been one of the most successful SaaS companies outside the US over time. And they’ve kept it up. Today, 49% of their ARR is from outside North America. A reminder to go global as early and often as you can.
#4.  Monday.com’s Revenue Growth Has Slowed But Not Too Much
Monday still has epic growth — but it isn’t growing quite at the same rate as in 2021-22. It was up a stunning 50%+ last year, but that is down to “only” +17% this year. Still pretty darn good.
#5.  Monday.com’s Gross Margins Have Fallen From 80% to 77%. A Little More Than Expected
Monday.com has been one of the most profitable SaaS companies for years and years — with gross margins at a stunning 80%-85%. But like so many others, they’re now back down to ~75%-80%.

answer:
So one thing we don’t talk too much about on SaaStr is “M&A”.  It’s not that big a deal in the end.  But it can be an important part of your journey as CEO and Founder.
I’ve personally been through three M&As:
One at $2m (a small VC backed company sold to a bigger player)
One at $20m
And one just before IPO, where we were acquired by Oracle for $800m.  It was worth it.
The reason I wrote about Informatica here is that there’s an interesting case study in M&A with the data and analytics space.
Informatica has been around 32 years!  That’s even longer than me!
It was founded back when I first got into SaaS, so we kind of saw each other on the way up together.  It IPO’d once (as it did last week) and then sold to Perot Systems for $1.5B in 2008.
Then … it went bankrupt in 2012.
A year later Informatica was back on its feet with a new CEO, but it took several more years to get back on track.  And by that point, the data management space had been disrupted forever by cloud and SaaS leaders like Salesforce, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud Platform (GCP).
So … after another 8+ years of steady growth …
In July 2023, Informatica announced it would be acquired for $8 billion by
Salesforce.  This is the biggest acquisition in Salesforce’s history.
And to make things even more interesting, this IPO was actually its second one!  After selling out to Perot Systems back in 2009 and then being taken private (i.e., “de-listed”) from NASDAQ — it went public again!
In fact, I’m not sure if it has any real competitors left.

So much can happen over 32 years. And so much did with Informatica.
Started as one of the first data integration products back in 1993
Survived a near-death experience in ’06 when Oracle nearly acquired it for pennies on the dollar (it was valued at $1 billion and they wanted to pay just $300M)
Had its second IPO in 2015, raised another $450M, got into Cloud data integration. But didn’t really catch fire
Then Salesforce came knocking with a $9B bid that Informatica accepted — but then the deal fell apart (it was worth ~$10B at closing) after it became clear they weren’t going to get regulatory approval in Europe
Informatica went private again, eventually selling for $5.3B to Permira and others in 2015, before becoming a public company once more in 2020 with a market cap of over $2 billion
Fast forward to today: Salesforce is buying Informatica for ~$8 Billion
This deal isn’t just about getting its hands on Informatica’s data integration assets. It’s also about going head-to-head against Oracle and others.
What can we learn here? A few things:
First, in SaaS, there are no permanent winners or losers — not really anyway. But you have to play the game 32 years if you want a shot at it all.
Second, if you’re in SaaS, be careful about getting too big for your britches. Oracle tried (and failed) twice. Salesforce is trying now with this deal. It

answer:
So for me, at least as an observer, the last year and a half has been the biggest change I’ve seen in B2B sales since the early days. The shift from enterprise to SMB is real.  Salesforce’s big push into “smaller” businesses is also real. But both are still just niches.
But what’s happened recently that isn’t niche, at least for many of us? More and more folks buying SaaS apps on a credit card now.
No one had predicted this in 2020-21 when we were all forced into Zoom calls with no time to talk sales. But it seems like an awful lot of folks are doing just that today — they’re paying up front for most deals, but also not waiting to close the deal if they can afford it on a credit card.
And then … more and more folks buying SaaS apps themselves now. Without anyone else in their company even knowing about it.
This is huge, because sales has always been at least somewhat driven by the internal politics of every organization.
So what’s changing here? Why are we seeing so much change all at once?
The main driver here I think for many folks and companies is a “forced” shift to smaller deals in enterprise. When you were used to $300k+ ACV deal, it was a big deal. You went through multiple rounds of due diligence with procurement and legal.
But these days? More and more everyone wants to buy SaaS apps now. On their own credit card even! And they want to do it fast.
So we’re seeing all sorts of changes here:
A lot more deals are being closed in just a few weeks, if not less than 30. A lot more folks buying on their own without anyone else involved
More and more “smaller” businesses using Salesforce as an example to buy from the enterprise leaders
And for sure — credit cards have become a very common way of paying.
These are all big changes to traditional sales processes, at least in my lifetime.

So we’ve been doing some investing lately at our new $500m fund at SaaStr Fund.
It’s always fun to invest with your friends and co-investors.  Especially when they can give you a second opinion as things develop. It also keeps the bar high — no one is going to want to be a dumb investor in anyone that works with them too much! 🙂

I think the answer to this question is “they shouldn’t be.”
The only time VCs worry is when no one seems willing to pay it.  When in fact everyone wants to buy at some insane multiple — say 100x or so.
In that case, they are worried because there’s no way to get their money out of the company.

answer:
If you are an SaaS CEO and your Net New Customer growth is less than $10M, then you have at least one big issue.  In fact, it’s likely two.
First, that means your base is not growing quickly enough
Second, the problem is compounded by the other: you’re not able to invest in new features and functionality fast enough to attract new customers. And if your NRR isn’t strong — well then, you just have a few years at best.
If nothing else, don’t do anything but fix this one thing first:
Get Your Growth Up.  Now.  Whatever it Takes.
But what can we do once we are in the situation?  What should we do to reverse NRR zombiesm?
First of all — if your NNR is high and you’re doing well with new customers, I wouldn’t make a huge change here.  You know why?  Because it’s working.
But, but … what about when it isn’t? What about when NRR has gone down from say +100% to just +40%, or even lower?
Well — first of all, be honest with yourself:
Are you in a state of “NRR Zombie” ?
If your Net Retention Rate is below 110% and growing slower than new customers … then yes.  You are in an NRR zombie.
Then ask yourself one question:
What am I going to do about it?
Because at some point, all the excuses run out.  All of them.  You can’t blame the competition anymore once you’re in this state.  You can’t say your product isn’t good enough — because then what?  You just give up and go home?  Not really.
So ask yourself:
What am I going to do about it?
And … well, if nothing else, at least fix the obvious issues first.
Fix Your Support
.  It may not be broken (but is probably worse than you think), but your support team isn’t magical — they can only help so many folks per month.  So get a lot more of them.  And better ones.
Get Better At Onboarding
.  Because if it’s hard to use, no one wants to buy from you.
Do More Marketing and Sales
.  Even if it doesn’t seem like it will work — because your base is so small and NRR low.  Because that’s the only way to get more customers in this case.
Go all-in on upsells for now
.  If nothing else, at least go all-in here — even if you know later that these new features won’t be worth it.

A few weeks. But here’s what you really need to know:
You can’t just buy some AI tool, train it on your existing email database and expect magical results.
The best tools use natural language processing (NLP) plus a ton of domain knowledge specific to sales development. start by using some AI SDR tools for just 1-2 days as an “experiment”. Don’t commit to anything yet.

if you have a good database, then the training process should take around 7-10 days with full automation (you probably need human review and validation of each output).

once it’s working — keep feeding in new data. The AI will get smarter over time as long as your team is using it.

if you don’t have a great database, then the training process can take months. This isn’t really an “AI SDR” anymore — more like just another tool that doesn’t work very well.
And here’s what I see almost no one do:
You need to be using AI SDR tools for real every single day if you want them to actually get any good at it.
If your team is only logging in once a week, then the thing isn’t getting better. It’ll just keep spitting out mediocre results over and over again.

I don’t think you should use any sort of automated outbound for the most part until it’s proven to work. And that only works with folks who have done this before.
First, if your team hasn’t done outbound sales (and really even inbound) before — they won’t know how to make an AI SDR work.  The data, the sequences, the follow-up are all critical.  An AI doesn’t understand these nuances and subtleties in most cases.
Secondly, it’s hard enough getting a human outbound motion going. It takes a lot of time — months really — to get good at it if you don’t have any experience with it. A Human SDR isn’t magical. You can make the numbers work with 10-15 qualified reps closing deals (and that usually requires about $1m in sales and marketing spending). But getting there is hard.
And thirdly, a lot of folks are doing this now — running AI outbound before they have a real working human motion. And it’s just not really working out as well as everyone hoped.  You can’t get enough qualified leads from an AI SDR to justify 2 people on the team full-time. They’re trying, but most of them aren’t getting there yet.
So unless you already have a proven outbound process — don’t do this. It’s not worth it. Don’t let folks sell you on some fancy “AI outbound” solution that sounds good in theory. Unless they’ve actually done it before and can show you the results, don’t bother trying to get an AI SDR going until you have a working human motion first.

So we had to do a major upgrade of our SaaS product at end-of-year, and Ava didn’t work with it until December 28th. So from December 29th through January 3rd … it didn’t work. It couldn’t connect or login. And then on January 4th — it just worked again.

And now we’ve got to do some deep cleaning on how everything is set up. A lot of it was still working fine — but not all of it. And that’s a problem for us now. It would have been easy to fix back in December 2025, when the product change happened. But no one did.
The bottom line:
You can’t train an AI agent and then just … go away. You need someone at least part-time keeping up with how it all works. And making sure that agents are still working well across your workflows and tools.

The Cowan Paradox isn’t just true for work — it’s also happening in our personal lives
When AI agents make us more efficient at home (and we’re getting things done faster), the bar goes up again. We need to produce even higher quality output, whether that means cooking a perfect meal or writing a compelling email.

answer:
So I’ve been doing this SaaS thing for over 15 years now, and it has changed so much.
It’s still huge.  It is a multi-trillion dollar industry today, growing at epic rates, with no end in sight.
But … but the way we used to win? The way we used to be successful?
That’s gone.
So let me make this clear: I love AI and apps as much as anyone else.  And that will continue for a long time.  But there are two things you need to know if you’re trying to build something in B2B today, or even just scale it from 1-10M ARR:
#1 — The “Old Way” of SaaS is Dead
You can’t win anymore by being cheaper.  It’s dead.
In fact, AI has made this worse than ever before.  You need to be better and faster in B2B today … with lower costs.  But that doesn’t mean you have to go cheap.  That just means going all-in on automation and AI.  And if your margins are too low — then maybe there is no room for any of this.
You can’t win anymore by being a feature list, or even a workflow tool.  It’s dead.
In fact, the more features you have … the less relevant you’ll be in B2B today.  Your competitors will just build them on top of AI and apps anyway.
The old way to win was cheap, with lots of features that worked well together for 1-10 people at a company.  Those days are gone.
#2 — The New Way is … Different
So what’s the new way?
It’s not quite sure yet, but we know it involves AI and apps in some fashion.  And the winners will be:
The best integrators of everything that works in AI today.  That’s a lot harder than it sounds.
The fastest to market with real value — from day 1, even if you have limited features and an unpolished interface.
This is really hard.
